Camera trap deployments—particularly in dense understory habitats preferred by muntjac—should be configured to capture activity during early morning and late evening hours to maximize detection probability.

However, practical visibility may vary: dense vegetation in spring and summer can obstruct camera views, potentially reducing detection rates even when animals are present.
Detectability may thus be highest in autumn and early spring, when vegetation is sparse

Barkin: This offers an additional opportunity for detection: passive acoustic monitoring using audio recorders can serve as a complement to camera-based surveillance, particularly in habitats where visual detection is impaired.
Because barking is loud, repetitive, and species-specific, it may provide a reliable cue including in conditions where camera traps may be less effective.\

Statistical modeling: The most important implications concern replication of observations:\
The estimation/identification of random effects requires multiple measures within the predictor to be included via a random effect (e.g., repeated measures within a grid cell or measurement site).
Also, the estimation of the detection probability requires repeated measures at a specific site.

### Additional considerations

Monitoring to evaluate management:\
Monitoring in relation to management ranges on a continuum with as end points estimating causal effects (sometimes also called the effectiveness) of measurement actions versus measuring their temporal and spatial correlates.
The degree of experimental and/or statistical control (in conjunction with more or less strong assumptions) determines the position on this continuum, and thus to what extent observed changes in, for example, population size can directly or indirectly be attributed to actions taken.
Throughout this report we use the formulation ‘monitoring under management’ to indicate that any monitoring scheme will likely be closer to the ‘temporal and spatial correlates’ endpoint of the above-mentioned continuum than to the ‘effectiveness’ endpoint.

Estimating causal effects of management actions is complicated: The number of shot animals might be relatively easy to assess, but effects can also be less direct.
For instance a population might not be eradicated immediately, but reduced to such a critical extent that this leads to a delayed collapse.
Such effects are usually mediated through other processes (e.g. if only bucks are left, sexual reproduction is blocked, leading to extinction).
Also, interactions with additional risk factors such as disease might but need not play a role.
Talking about additional factors, these can of course also on their own affect more distal variables such as the population size.
Hence, quantifying the total effect of a management action such as control through shooting on outcome variables such as population size while at the same time ruling out the effects of other factors with sufficient confidence requires experimental and/or statistical control.
Whereas the first is add odds with EU law and seems unethical, the latter usually draws on study design specifics and/or assumptions to emulate an experimental setup.
